subject: physics
title: Newton's Laws and Force Diagrams
welcome_lead: Apply Newton's three laws to analyse forces, accelerations and tension in connected systems.
meta_desc: A-Level Mechanics adventure on Newton's laws applied to dynamic systems.
final_note: F = ma is the bridge between forces you see and motion you predict.

concepts.def: Body stays at rest or constant velocity if F_net=0.
F_net = ma; force gives proportional acceleration.
Every action has equal and opposite reaction.
Gravitational force on a mass: W = mg.
Pulling force transmitted through a string.

walkthroughs.body_html: Isolate the object. Draw every force acting on it as arrows from the body. Resolve into convenient axes (often parallel and perpendicular to motion).
Two masses m1 and m2 over a pulley. Acceleration a = (m1 - m2)g / (m1 + m2). Tension T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2).
Weight component down a slope of angle theta is mg sin(theta). Normal force is mg cos(theta). Friction opposes motion.

mcqs.q: Which law explains why a rocket accelerates as it expels exhaust?
options: 1st Law
2nd Law
3rd Law
Hooke's Law

mcqs.q: Net force on an object moving at constant velocity is:
options: mg
zero
ma
maximum

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The force is in the same direction as the current in the wire.
The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.

mcqs.q: In what direction does a magnetic field exert a force on a current-carrying wire?
options: Perpendicular to both the current direction and the magnetic field direction (Fleming's left hand rule).
The force is in the same direction as the current in the wire.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
The force is in the same direction as the magnetic field.
